# Cūḷaseṭṭhijātaka (Ja 4)

**ID:** Ja 4
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷaseṭṭhijātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Tale of the Financier
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja4
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷaseṭṭhijātaka* (Ja 4) is the fourth story in the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its frame narrative, the Buddha related this account while dwelling in Jīvaka's mango grove near Rājagaha, occasioned by the elder Little Wayman (Cūḷapanthaka / Cūdapanthaka) [SuttaCentral; Swanson 2004]. The introductory story (*paccuppannavatthu*) shares close textual parallels with the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* account of Mahāpanthaka and Cūḷapanthaka on Dhp 25, recounting how the dull-witted novice struggled to memorize a single verse until the Buddha provided him with a simple practice leading to awakening and miraculous powers [Burlingame 1921; Swanson 2004].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta acts as a discerning financier who spots a dead mouse on the road and remarks that an energetic youth could use it to establish a business and maintain a household [Appleton 2010]. A poor young man overhears the Bodhisatta's advice, sells the dead mouse as cat meat, and through a sequence of shrewd, opportunistic ventures gradually amasses enormous wealth [Winternitz 1933; Nariman 1919; Appleton 2010]. Out of gratitude, he returns half his wealth to the Bodhisatta, who rewards him with his daughter's hand in marriage [Appleton 2010].

While DharmaNexus records no Pali-internal reuse or cross-language matches scoring 10 or higher [DharmaNexus], scholars have identified extensive parallels across South Asian and Buddhist narrative literature. The story of acquiring a fortune from a dead rodent corresponds directly to an episode in the Sanskrit *Divyāvadāna* (pp. 498–499) [Cowell and Neil 1886; Winternitz 1933; Nariman 1919; Rotman 2017]. Related versions also occur in the Tibetan and Chinese translations of the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayavibhaṅga*, as well as in the non-Buddhist narrative cycle of the *Kathāsaritsāgara* (1.6) [Cowell and Neil 1886; Rotman 2017].
